_comment_rock_form: OF11. The rises' rock FORM, and a replacement for -- not an extension of -- `colour.relief_amplitude`/`relief_frequency`, which were removed. Those added one smooth FBM bump to a smooth analytic cone; a blind critic on the result still read 'a single smooth, continuous, unbroken curve,' and five rounds before that only ever repainted the same dome. Smooth noise cannot produce stone at any amplitude: FBM's extrema are rounded, so its surfaces are swells, and a swell painted grey is a stain. This block builds the two things a rock hillside actually has and a swell does not, both of them DISCONTINUITIES: creased ribs and gullies (a RIDGED fractal, domain-warped so the ribs meander and pinch out rather than tiling) and bedding planes (`terrace_*`, which quantises the rise's own height into near-level ledges separated by steep risers -- the plateau in docs/reference/palworld-04 and the crags in the key art are made of exactly this). See playground_heightfield.gd::_rise_relief. Everything here is faded out at the rim (`rim_in`/`rim_out`) so `rises` alone still decides each landform's footprint and the roads at its foot are untouched. ALL TUNABLE.

rock_form._comment_amplitude: Metres of rib/gully relief at full gate. The previous layer's last attempt was 2.5m and read as nothing from 60-95m out; this is proportionate to a 78m-radius, 46m-tall landform. TUNABLE: too high and the rise stops reading as one hill.
rock_form._comment_frequency: Round 2: was 0.028 (~36m between ribs). The round-1 critic read the ribs as "corduroy... the same scalloped sawtooth at identical frequency and amplitude across the entire dome"; evenly-spaced ribs at a single scale are exactly what a single-frequency ridged field makes. Fewer, larger ribs (~53m) with more contrast between octaves gives one dominant rib system with smaller ones hanging off it, which is what a hillside's drainage actually looks like.
rock_form._comment_bias: Subtracted from the ridged value, so gullies cut deeper than ribs stand proud. Erosion removes material; without this the layer would inflate the rise as well as texture it.
rock_form._comment_warp: Domain warp on the coordinates the ridged field is sampled at. Unwarped ridged noise is recognisably even-spaced and isotropic; this makes the ribs meander, converge and pinch out.
rock_form._comment_round3: Round 3. Two blind critics in a row named the same defect: 'identical sawtooth grooves at identical spacing and identical depth, wrapped uniformly around the whole dome... every groove is the same tooth.' The teeth are a resonance between a near-vertical bed boundary and a carve field with one dominant wavelength, so the fix is to detune it rather than to shrink it. `bed_fracture` is a SECOND, finer wobble on the bed boundary (~12m against `bed_wobble`'s ~35m) so an outcrop edge is ragged at two scales and no single tooth size is recognisable; `bed_thickness_jitter` varies bed thickness through a deliberately non-integer cycle (playground_heightfield.gd::BED_CYCLE) so no two adjacent beds match and the stack never repeats; `terrace_riser` 0.34 -> 0.5 and `terrace_strength` 0.5 -> 0.4 turn the risers from a comb back into ledges. `rubble_amplitude` is separate: metre-scale creases sampled from the same ridged field at 3.4x the coordinate rate, for the critic's other finding at close range -- 'zero surface micro-detail, no grain, no crumble.' ALL TUNABLE.
rock_form._comment_terrace: Bedding planes. `terrace_height` is metres of elevation per bed. `terrace_riser` is the fraction of each bed that is the steep riser rather than the near-level ledge; smaller is sharper. `terrace_strength` blends the terraced height against the un-terraced one, so 1.0 is a full staircase and 0 is off. `bed_dip` is the whole point of round 2: metres of rise per metre of world X and Z, i.e. the TILT of the bedding planes. Round 1 terraced a quantity that depends only on radius, so every bed outcropped as a concentric circle at one elevation -- a wedding cake -- and the blind critic read it as 'corduroy, not erosion... the same scalloped sawtooth at identical frequency and amplitude across the entire dome.' [0.34,-0.19] leans the beds about 21 degrees across the hill, so a bed surfaces high on one flank and low on the other and the rings become long diagonal bands, which is what a stratified hill actually shows. `bed_wobble` (fractions of a bed) warps the planes with the `_outcrop` field so they are not flat either -- thick beds here, thin there, the difference between sedimentary rock and a stack of coins. TUNABLE: this whole group is the strongest 'reads as stone' lever in the file, and `terrace_strength`/`bed_dip` are the first two places to look if the rise starts reading as a staircase again.
rock_form._comment_curvature: Read only by `rock_bias_deg`, not by the geometry: the step at which the relief field's convexity is sampled, and how many metres of convexity count as fully convex. `curvature_step` should stay well under `terrace_height`'s horizontal span or the riser lips stop resolving.
rock_form._comment_rim: The only gate. Zero at the rim so each rise's footprint and the ground the roads run over are exactly what `rises` says; full from 18% of the radius inward, summit INCLUDED -- unlike the old relief layer, which switched itself off at the summit and left a grass cap on what both reference boards draw as a rock crag.

routes._comment_of10a: OF10a (walkability half of OF10). The old last two points (85,-48) and (118,-72) drove this road in a straight line up and OVER `rises.peaks[0]`'s own rim -- fine for the first ~38m of that line (slope <=6 deg the whole way, `tools/`-style probe with slope_degrees_at at 0.5m steps) and then a genuine cliff: 4.8deg at (76.9,-42.7) to 46.4deg just 1.2m later at (78.1,-43.5), and 40-52deg for most of the rest of the climb toward both old points -- well past the player's own 45deg floor_max_angle (player.tscn), so the character simply cannot walk it, in any direction, not just straight ahead (confirmed with a headless playthrough: holding forward pins the player exactly at the base of this same jump, is_on_floor never leaves true, velocity pins at zero). This is the rise's own DESIGNED collar (terrain_playground.json's own `rises` comment: 'these are the only places the 45-degree slope limit should actually bite'; EV4-hillside-seam-remainder-4's `relief_amplitude`/`relief_frequency`, gated to this exact flank band and owned by the separate look-quality item, add further sub-2m irregularity on top of it) -- not a collision defect like OF6's undersized boundary box, and not something this item's own scope may touch (rises.peaks / relief are geometry the look pass already tuned against). A grid pathfind at up to 2m resolution could not thread a >=44deg-safe line through that collar anywhere near this bearing; the two are genuinely entangled, per this item's own escape valve. The walkable fix is where the road ITSELF stops: truncated to end at (74,-41), the last point on the ORIGINAL bearing/line before the cliff (worst slope on the new leg is 13.3deg, with the cliff still 4-6m further on) -- 82.2m from the rise's own centre, i.e. just past the dome's 78m-radius footprint, so the road now reads as reaching the genuine foot of the rise and stopping there, not dead-ending mid-slope. Nothing in `rises`, `colour.relief_*`, or any texture/material entry was touched.

A crossing owns three things at once and they have to agree, which is why they are one entry rather than three: the `road` polyline (unioned into playground_heightfield.road_polylines(), so the bake paints the same trodden soil along it and the scatter keeps grass and trees off it, exactly as a spoke road gets), the `carve` that interrupts it (the same straight-trench profile `_carve_depth` evaluates for every spoke gorge and the pond outlet -- one falloff evaluator on this map), and the `bridge` that is the only way over. _comment_drains: D41, debuted by SD16 at the Old Quarry. Team Tether's hardware is pulling something out of the ground and the ground shows it: discoloured, desaturated earth and suppressed vegetation in a radius around every station, thinning toward the machine and healthy meadow resuming past it. This block is the ONE authored source for where that happens. `playground_heightfield.drain_factor()` reads it and returns 0..1, and all three consumers ask that one function -- the bake's colour map (a tint lerp), the bake's control map (a blend toward the dead-soil texture) and `scatter_rules.gd` (which thins each layer's placements by its own `drain_suppression`). Same contract shape as `path_factor`/`stream_factor`/`building_apron_factor`, and the same reason for it: three systems agreeing about one edge because they read one function. D41 says mild at this rung of 32's reveal ladder -- the quarry's own head station is 0.85 and the run out of it falls away to 0.5, against the relay (SE23), which is meant to be the worst thing the player has seen. Widening these radii is how a later station gets worse; a new grammar is not. ALL TUNABLE.

drains._comment_strength: A global multiplier over every station below, for turning the whole effect down (or off, at 0) in one place while judging a render. Not a per-station knob -- those are per-station.
drains._comment_tint: The colour map MULTIPLIES the PBR albedo (see this file's own `_comment_colour`), so this is deliberately not far below the near-white the healthy bands use -- most of the dead read comes from the control map swapping the pixel to bare soil below, and a much darker tint here would be a brightness change pretending to be a colour, which is the exact mistake that comment exists to prevent. Desaturated and slightly warm-grey: sun-killed ground, not ash.
drains._comment_control_strength: How far a fully drained pixel blends toward the `soil` texture. Not 1.0: at this rung the ground is dying, not dead, and leaving a fraction of the grass texture showing through is the difference between 'this is going wrong' and 'this is a dirt patch'.

_comment_drains_relay_bake: HONEST PARTIAL, SE23. The three `relay_*` stations above are authored here, in the one place drains are authored, and `playground_heightfield.drain_factor()` reads them like every other station. TWO of that function's three consumers are already live from this edit alone: `scatter_rules.gd` thins the vegetation at run time (the ground around the relay is genuinely bald the moment the game boots) and anything else asking the function gets the right answer. _comment_spokes: SA4. Seven old roads leaving the Meadows, each severed. Spec 1E ('the Meadows perimeter should visibly contain seven outward routes') and 29 ('Team Tether did not build seven random dead-end roads. They severed existing connections'). The layout rule that follows from 29 is the whole reason this is data and not seven hand-placed props: a spoke is a ROAD that runs the full way out from the village square and then STOPS at something the world can show, with land still visible past it. Never a wall built across a bearing. Bearings were chosen against the geography that already exists rather than spaced evenly on a compass -- the water spoke leaves through the valley the pond already sits in, the fire spoke climbs toward `rises.peaks[1]`, the air spoke runs onto `rises.peaks[0]`'s flank -- so the blockers stand where the ground already justifies them. HARD RULE, from the backlog item and spec 19: nothing here may ever explain itself with UI text. The signs are old destination fingerposts (29's 'old signs'), naming where the road USED to go; none of them says the road is closed.
_comment_spokes_radius: Blockers sit at ~160-200m from the origin, INSIDE `world_perimeter.gd`'s 235m boundary ring, not astride it. Two reasons. The ring is one continuous ground-sampled polyline whose collision boxes are generated from the same points (see that file's OF7 header) -- cutting seven openings into it to put a blocker in each is a rebuild of a system that was rebuilt once already because it was not continuous. And a severed road reads better with meadow still running past it: the player walks up to the gorge, sees the roadbed resume on the far rim, and the boundary they eventually reach off to the side is an ordinary field edge rather than the story. TUNABLE.
_comment_spokes_schema: Per entry: `id` (node name and log key), `type` (the biome the road pointed at -- data only, nothing reads it yet), `bearing_deg` (atan2(z,x) in degrees, recorded so the layout is auditable without re-deriving it from the points), `road` (polyline in world metres from the village square outward; unioned into `paths` by playground_heightfield so the bake paints real soil along it, the scatter keeps vegetation off it, and path-anchored stone scatter follows it -- WITHOUT adding an arm to the village junction signpost, which reads `paths.routes` only), `sign` (optional; one fingerpost through signpost.gd's `routes_override`, same object as `paths.trailheads`), `blocker` (`kind` plus that kind's own fields), and `built` (false = authored but not yet standing; severed_spokes.gd skips it). Blocker kinds: `gorge` and `collapsed_bridge` both carry a `carve` and are cut into the TERRAIN at bake time; `rockslide` is props and collision only and needs no re-bake.

spokes._comment_carve: A carve is a straight trench in the heightfield: local u runs along `axis_deg`, v across it. Full `depth` within `half_width` of the axis, fading to nothing over `rim` -- so the wall angle is roughly atan(depth/rim) and must stay well past the player's 45-degree floor_max_angle for the carve to be the blocker. Full depth within `half_length` of `centre` along u, fading out over `end_fade` so the trench does not stop with a squared-off wall in open grass. Subtracted after the flats and alongside the stream carve (playground_heightfield.height_at).

colour._comment_soil_slope_of11: OF11: back to 30 from EV4-hillside-seam-remainder's 24. colour._comment_rock_slope_of11_r2: OF11 round 2 tried 44 -> 48 and round 3 reversed past it to 42 -- 48 made the visible flank 46% SOIL, and a blind critic read the whole landform as "a plain khaki dome" and "scorched late-summer scrub": warm tan Ground003 over most of the face is the opposite of reading as stone. At 42 against `soil_slope_deg` 34, a flank sitting at 40-55 degrees is mostly ROCK, soil is the thin band where a ledge's turf gives out, and grass holds the ledges themselves -- green ledges, stone risers, which is what the key art's hilltop crag actually looks like. Original round-2 note follows. Round 2: 44 -> 48. With `rock_form`'s bedding planes the lower flank alternates ledge and riser, and at 44 the risers AND most of the un-terraced flank between them crossed into rock -- the round-1 render came out 39% rock across peaks[0]'s footprint, a bare hill. TUNABLE.
colour._comment_blend_deg_rock: OF11 round 6. The band-ramp width ON THE RISES, interpolated against `blend_deg` above by build_playground_terrain.gd::_band_blend — the same rise/meadow split `slope_sample_step_rock` already uses, and for the same underlying reason. `blend_deg` is a width in DEGREES, but what a viewer sees is a width in METRES, and round 4 deliberately made slope change very fast on the rises by sampling it at 2m instead of 6m. Out on the meadow 6 degrees of ramp is several metres of gradual transition; across a `rock_form` riser the same 6 degrees is crossed inside a pixel or two, so the ramp collapses and the boundary bakes as a hard edge — which is what the round-5 blind critic reported: the moss/dirt patches 'meet bare stone in hard stencil-edged shapes with no organic blend... a stencil laid over the rock, not moss actually growing in a crevice.' That is a side effect of round 4's win, not a regression in it, so the fix widens the ramp only where the slope field is steep and leaves both the meadow and the fine sampling alone. 8.0 is the CEILING, not a preference: `_control_for` needs `soil_slope_deg + blend <= rock_slope_deg` to keep its five bands from overlapping, and that gap is 42-34 = 8. Raising this further does nothing until those two move apart; the function clamps rather than letting the bands collapse. TUNABLE.
colour._comment_outcrop_detail: OF11 round 6, and the other half of the stencil-edge fix — the half that does the real work, since `blend_deg_rock` only had 2 degrees of headroom to give. `outcrop_jitter_*` above runs at ~35m and decides where the rock band bulges into a LOBE; it cannot do anything about the EDGE of that lobe, which at 35m is a smooth vector curve however many lobes it makes. A turf/stone boundary is ragged at the scale of the turf, so this second field runs at ~3.6m (frequency 0.28) with 3 octaves and breaks the boundary into interlocking fingers of moss and stone instead of a cut line. Gated to the rises by `rise_form_factor` inside playground_heightfield.gd::rock_bias_deg, deliberately NOT folded into `outcrop_jitter_deg`: at this wavelength an ungated 4 degrees would ride the open meadow's own grass/soil threshold and speckle soil across flat ground, which is the blotching `slope_sample_step` exists to suppress. TUNABLE: amplitude is the raggedness, frequency is the finger size; lower the frequency if the edge starts reading as noise rather than as growth.
colour._comment_slope_sample_step_rock: OF11 round 4. The band pick's slope sample step ON THE RISES, interpolated against `slope_sample_step` above by playground_heightfield.gd::rise_form_factor. One global step cannot serve both places any more: 6m exists to low-pass the `detail` noise layer out on the open meadow (see `_comment_slope_sample_step`), and on a rise it low-passes away the ledges, riser lips and metre-scale creases `rock_form` builds -- so the material landed in soft blobs that ignored the crevices under them, which is exactly what the round-3 blind critic reported ('the dark olive patches have hard, rounded, blobby edges that don't track the crevice geometry underneath them... the bumps and the tint aren't talking to each other'). They were not talking because the pick was deaf at the scale the geometry speaks at. 2m resolves a terrace riser and a rib crest; the meadow keeps 6m and its blotching stays fixed. TUNABLE: lower for a tighter fit to the rock form, raise if the rise starts speckling.

_comment_wet_ev5: EV5. `wet_tint`/`wet_strength` darken the colour map toward damp sand wherever the ground is under or beside water (below `water.level` plus a fading ring ~0.7m above it, and inside the stream channel). This DELIBERATELY dips below the '#c0 floor' rule above -- that rule exists to stop accidental brightness-as-colour, and a wet bed being darker than dry ground is the intended read, not an accident: it is half of the shallow-edge colour shift the water shader's own depth gradient carries the other half of. At 0.5 strength the multiply bottoms out around #dfd0b8 over the near-white greens, a modest dip. TUNABLE.
_comment_of11_band: OF11. `rock_exposure_deg`/`rock_curvature_deg`/`rock_crown_deg`/`rock_crown_range` replace slope-plus-noise as the rule for WHERE rock shows (playground_heightfield.gd::rock_bias_deg, read by both bake passes). Every earlier round picked the band from slope alone plus `outcrop_jitter_deg`; on a smooth cone slope is a pure function of radius, so rock could only ever be a ring and the jitter only made it a lobed ring -- the material and the surface under it were describing different objects, which is what 'rock reads as a stain, not stone' means. These three read the rise's OWN relief field instead: `rock_exposure_deg` follows its sign so ribs get rock and gullies keep soil/grass, `rock_curvature_deg` follows its local convexity so crests and terrace-riser lips go to rock while the inside corner at a ledge's foot holds soil the way scree and turf really gather, and `rock_crown_deg` bares the summit, which both reference boards draw as rock and this terrain drew as grass. `outcrop_jitter_deg` stays but is halved (6.0 -> 3.0): it is now residual break-up on top of a structural rule rather than the only thing making the ring irregular. ALL TUNABLE -- raise `rock_crown_deg` for more bare summit, `rock_exposure_deg` for a stronger rib/gully split, `rock_curvature_deg` for crisper edges where rock meets soil.
_comment_ev4_hillside_seam_remainder_4_s: SUPERSEDED by OF11 -- `relief_amplitude`/`relief_frequency` no longer exist; `rock_form` above replaces them. Kept because it records the last of the five rounds this item was told not to continue. EV4-hillside-seam-remainder-4. `relief_amplitude`/`relief_frequency` are new and different in kind from every lever above: those all repaint the SAME smooth dome differently (tint, band thresholds, which band a slope reading picks); this perturbs the dome's own HEIGHT, gated to each rise's flank only (playground_heightfield.gd::_rise_height's own `flank` smoothstep window -- zero at the summit, zero at the rim, so the rise's footprint and peak height are unchanged). Three colour-only rounds moved the paint without moving a blind critic's verdict ('two materials, not three; rock reads as a stain, not stone') because a slope reading from a perfectly smooth surface can only ever fake a material change, never show one. relief_frequency 0.07 (~14m wavelength) is close-grained relief within one rise, not another lobe-scale undulation like outcrop_jitter_frequency's ~35m. First attempt: relief_amplitude 0.8m, chosen conservatively so test_there_is_somewhere_steep_enough_to_matter's slope-fraction bounds and the landform's own probed max slope (~52 degrees, see blend_deg_r2's comment) stayed comfortably inside range. Direct probing (sampling height_at/slope_degrees_at along the flank) confirmed the noise was genuinely active, not a no-op -- real non-monotonic slope wobble in the gated zone -- but a fresh blind critic still called the silhouette 'a single smooth, continuous, unbroken curve' in all three frames: 0.8m of relief on a landform with 72m of total height range and a 78m-radius rise is proportionally too small to read from viewing distance, even though it is real. Raised to 2.5m -- still well inside the slope-fraction bounds (probed) -- as this lever's second and, per this item's own done-when, likely final attempt before a geometry lever this size is judged exhausted too. TUNABLE.
_comment_blend_deg_r2: EV4-hillside-seam round 2 (was 7.0, tried 14.0), round 3 (blend 8.0, rock_slope_deg 44.0 -> 40.0), round 4 (blend 6.0, rock_slope_deg back to 44.0). Round 2 doubled blend_deg to fix a round-1 critic's 'hard, unblended seam' complaint, but pushed pure rock's threshold (rock_slope_deg + blend_deg) to 58 degrees, outside this landform's own reachable slope -- probed directly with tools/debug_slope_probe.gd against `rises.peaks[0]` (centre [140,-90], radius 78, the exact landform capture_hillside.gd frames), this rise's slope peaks at ~52.5 degrees around 72m out along the east bearing and then RECEDES toward its base skirt. Round 3 fixed that by lowering rock_slope_deg to 40, which worked -- rock became visible -- but overcorrected the other way: a fresh blind critic reported rock now DOMINATES two of three frames (60-75% of the visible hill) and there is still no distinct soil band, because blend=8 left only a 2-degree pure-soil plateau (38-40), too thin to read as a third material at these camera distances. Round 4 keeps blend NARROWER (6.0, between round 2's failed 14.0 and the original 7.0) and restores rock_slope_deg to its original pre-EV4-hillside-seam value (44.0) rather than lowering it again, which together open an 8-degree pure-soil plateau (36-44, versus round 3's 2) while pushing pure rock back to 50 degrees -- the probe shows that band occurs only from roughly 68m to 74m out, a narrow accent ring near the base rather than a dominant face. TUNABLE; if soil still doesn't read as distinct, the plateau needs to be wider still (soil_slope_deg itself is the next lever, not touched by any of these four rounds); if rock has become too rare again, rock_slope_deg is the lever, not blend_deg -- round 3 already showed widening blend without checking landform-max-slope is how this regresses.
_comment_ev4_hillside_seam_remainder: EV4-hillside-seam-remainder. `soil_slope_deg` 30 -> 24 widens the pure-soil plateau from round 4's 8 degrees (36-44) to 14 (30-44) without moving `rock_slope_deg`, so rock's own share of the hill (round 4 already tuned to a narrow accent ring, not the round-3 dominant face) is untouched -- this is the 'plateau needs to be wider still' half of round 4's own next-step note. `outcrop_jitter_deg`/`outcrop_jitter_frequency` are new: every band pick used to be a pure function of slope, so a roughly circular rise baked a perfectly circular ring of soil and rock -- a 'collar,' per the round-4 critic, not an authored outcrop. `playground_heightfield.gd::outcrop_jitter_deg()` adds a coarse, seeded noise value (see its own comment) to the sampled slope before the band lookup, so the ring bulges into lobes in some directions and recedes in others instead of tracing one smooth circle. Symmetric around 0 (does not change the AVERAGE amount of rock or soil, only where each band's edge falls), so it is additive to the plateau widening above rather than a competing lever. TUNABLE: raise `outcrop_jitter_deg` for chunkier, more separated outcrops; lower `outcrop_jitter_frequency` for fewer, larger lobes.
_comment_slope_sample_step: EV4-hillside-seam. The grass/soil/rock band is picked from slope, and slope was sampled with the SAME 1m central-difference step as the geometry itself -- so every texture decision saw the `detail` noise layer's own ripple (frequency 0.018, ~14m at its highest FBM octave, amplitude enough to swing slope roughly +-14 degrees) on top of the actual macro shape. Against a 7-degree blend_deg that ripple is bigger than the band it is supposed to smooth, so a rise's flank does not read as one coherent ring per material -- it reads as whichever material the local noise happened to push slope past THIS pixel, over and over, which is the 'camouflage' pattern a blind critic named twice (EV4 round 3, EV4-hillside-seam). Sampling slope at a wider step low-passes exactly that ripple while leaving the geometry, collision and vegetation placement (scatter_rules.gd calls slope_degrees_at with its own default step) untouched -- this value is read ONLY by build_playground_terrain.gd's two texture bakes. TUNABLE: too small and the blotching returns, too large and the band stops following the rise's own shape and reads as a smeared ring.
_comment_shader: Terrain3D shader settings. Every one of these is TUNABLE presentation and none of them touches collision or height — the bake is authored data and this is only how it is drawn.

shader._comment_background: 2 = NOISE. It was 1 = FLAT, which draws an infinite plane at y=0 past the baked 512m and fogs it to a uniform sheet. That produced a measured 0.146 luminance step across the ENTIRE width of `03-rise-overlook` at row 252 — the blind critic found it independently and called it the first thing the eye lands on. Noise gives the distance real shape instead, so the world stops having a visible edge.
shader._comment_world_noise_removed: world_noise_scale/height/region_blend/lod_distance/max_octaves/min_octaves are NOT real uniforms on this Terrain3D build — confirmed by dumping Terrain3DMaterial's actual _get_shader_parameters() keys directly (R7.1), which do not include any world_noise_* name. world_background=NOISE above is a real property and does apply; the background's shape beyond it is this build's fixed default, not tunable from here. Removed rather than left silently ignored, same reasoning as dual_scale below.
shader._comment_macro: Macro variation tints the ground at two large scales, which is the only thing that stops a 2K tile reading as tiling. The critic measured the previous ground as high-frequency mottled noise with 'no blade direction and no scale cue' — a texture repeating every few metres with nothing varying above that.
shader._comment_macro_multiply: These MULTIPLY the albedo — the shader does `macrov = mix(colour1, white, noise1); macrov *= mix(colour2, white, noise2)`. So they can only ever darken, and two mid-tones compound: the first attempt used #c6d18a and #8fa06a, which multiply out to roughly 0.47 at their overlap and took the near-field ground from luminance 0.124 to 0.054 — a black foreground in every frame. Keep both near white and let them tint, not shade. Anything below about #b0 here is a brightness change wearing a colour's clothes.
shader._comment_dual_scale_removed: Terrain3D's dual-scaling uniforms (dual_scale_texture/near/far/reduction) are NOT reachable through set_shader_param on this build — the shader only compiles them in behind a feature this API does not expose, and writing them returns quietly having done nothing. They were configured here for two rounds while the surveys came back byte-identical. `_apply_ground_shader` now reads every uniform back and warns by name, which is how this was finally caught.
shader._comment_auto_removed: auto_slope/auto_height_reduction (R7.1): also not real uniform names on this build, same check as world_noise_* above. There is no exposed control over the auto-shader's grass/rock slope threshold or blend softness in this Terrain3D version; `colour.blend_deg` above only softens the BAKED vertex-colour transition, a separate layer from the live auto-shader texture switch.
shader._comment_enable_macro: R7.1: macro_variation1/2 above were configured but never actually applied — enable_macro_variation defaults false and nothing set it true. blend_sharpness, mipmap_bias, macro_variation1/2 and noise1/2_scale/angle ARE real uniforms on this build (confirmed the same way, and separately confirmed to affect the render: forcing extreme values visibly changes the frame even though get_shader_param() reads them back as null after every set — the readback is unreliable on this build, not the write). The `ignored N setting(s)` warning below is therefore a false positive for exactly these seven keys; it stays because it is still correct about world_noise_*/auto_slope/auto_height_reduction, which really are dead.
shader._comment_macro_r9_4: R9.4. Was #eef0d8 / #d8dcc0 -- both tinted toward yellow-green, so macro variation was a third compounding saturation multiplier on top of the texture tint and the baked colour map. Neutralised: it still does its job (breaking up the tile's repeat period at low frequency) but it no longer pushes hue. The pair keeps a slight warm/cool split so the variation is still visible as variation.
shader._comment_blend_r9_4: R9.4. Was 0.62. The blind critic found the grass/soil boundary on frame 03's near hill stepping in visible 90-degree blocks -- the splatmap texel grid showing through -- and called it the most obvious bug in the set. Softer blending spreads that transition over more texels. TUNABLE; if the ground starts looking muddy where two materials meet, this went too far.

_comment_textures: Real PBR ground, replacing the `show_colormap` debug view that stood in for it from M1 to the first art pass. Terrain3D's auto shader picks texture 0 on walkable ground and texture 1 on slopes, so the grass/soil/rock intent the bake already encodes is expressed with albedo and normal detail instead of flat vertex colour. `uv_scale` is metres per tile: too large and the ground is mush at distance, too small and it visibly repeats.
_comment_uv_scale: Metres per tile is 1/uv_scale, so 0.34 tiles every ~3m. It was 0.18 (~5.5m), and at that size the near ground showed the photograph's own brown patches rather than its average — a green meadow with a brown foreground, reading as two materials. Tighter tiling averages to grass; too tight and it visibly repeats, which is what the macro variation and detiling above are for.
_comment_normal_depth: The most consequential number in this file. A photographic grass normal map at full strength turns most of its texels away from a 52-degree sun, and the ground within ~30m of the camera goes black — measured at luminance 0.071 against 0.27-0.60 across the references, with exactly the high-frequency mottled fizz the critic described. It flattens with distance because the mip average cancels the perturbation, which is why the far hills looked correct and the foreground did not. Raise it for more relief; if the near ground starts crushing to black again, this is the cause.
_comment_detiling: Rotates and shifts the tile per region so a 2K texture stops announcing its own repeat period. Together with the shader's macro variation, this is what separates 'ground material' from 'wallpaper'.

textures._comment_which_grass: Grass008, chosen by tools/rank_ground_textures.py rather than by eye — which is how the previous two were chosen and how both went wrong. Scored on the defect the critic actually named: long thin dark filaments, the 'cracked plates' signature. Grass008 measures 0.64 against Grass005's 4.37 — nearly seven times fewer — at the same luminance and saturation, so nothing downstream needed retuning.
textures.name: grass
textures._comment_normal_depth: Cut from 0.30 to 0.12. Flat, BOTH textures look like grass — the 'fractured plates with dark fissure lines' the critic measured were RELIEF, not albedo: a photographic normal map at a grazing view angle carves shadow valleys that read as cracks in stone, and mip averaging smears them into plates at distance. This is the knob for that, not the texture.
textures._comment_tint_r9_4: R9.4 — WHY THIS TINT LOOKS LIKE LAVENDER AND IS NOT A MISTAKE. albedo_color MULTIPLIES, and multiplying by a tinted colour can only ever RAISE saturation, never lower it. Grass008's own mean is RGB(0.393,0.516,0.168), saturation 0.675; the old chartreuse tint #b9cf82 took it to 0.796, the baked colour map took it to 0.859, and macro variation took it to 0.873. Three multipliers each tinted toward yellow-green, compounding. The blind critic measured the rendered result at 0.55-0.72 mean saturation against 0.40-0.46 for the Palworld references and 0.39 for this project's own key art, sampled foreground grass at 92% saturation, and called it 'the green of a snooker table'. To DESATURATE a green by multiplying, the tint must raise blue relative to green -- which is what makes it read as lavender in a colour picker while the product lands on the board's own olive. Solved so albedo x tint x colour map x macro sits at hue 70, saturation 0.564: the exact hue and saturation of palette.json's meadow.grass_olive (#7f8c3d), which was sampled off the key art board. Value drops 0.328 -> 0.199, which is deliberate -- the critic found NO pixel below luminance 117 in the darkest 5% of three frames, and a dark albedo is where a real value range starts. TUNABLE, but re-solve it rather than eyeballing it: tools/frame_stats.py measures the result.

textures.name: rock
textures._comment_uv_scale_of11: OF11, and the single largest reason this material never read as stone. Metres per tile is 1/uv_scale: 0.12 is one tile every 8.3 METRES — the whole 1024px photograph, veining and all, blown up to the size of a house. Across peaks[0]'s visible face that is about ten tiles, so at the capture distances every grain of stone detail in the source lands below a pixel and the material resolves to its own flat average: a smooth grey wash with soft edges, which is exactly what five rounds of blind critics kept describing and no tint, AO, normal-depth or photo-brightness change could ever have fixed. Nobody had looked at this number — the comment it replaced was copy-pasted verbatim from the grass entry (it even quotes grass's own 0.34/0.18 history, values this entry has never held). 0.46 is one tile every ~2.2m, close to grass's own ~1.8m, so the two materials agree about how big a metre is and the photo's veining is visible as veining. Detiling and macro variation below are what stop that many repeats reading as wallpaper. TUNABLE.
textures._comment_normal_depth: Rock keeps more relief than grass. A cliff face with no normal detail reads as painted, and it is not the surface the player stands on at close range.
textures._comment_of11_r5: OF11 round 5. `normal_depth` 0.45 -> 0.6, paired with tools/art_pipeline/contrast_rock_texture.py restoring this photo's own local contrast (value std 0.058 -> 0.135, mean and hue held). Rounds 3 and 4 both accepted the LANDFORM as sculpted and both named the MATERIAL at close range instead -- 'a fine, even, low-contrast speckle with no strata, no cracks, no distinct rock chunks or slabs.' That is measurable and was measurably true: every lever this material has ever been given moves toward flatter (brightening raises the floor, cutting normal_depth and ao_strength removes shading, desaturating removes range), and in five pre-OF11 rounds plus OF11's own first four nobody had ever pushed the other way on the photograph itself. See that script's header. TUNABLE; if the rock starts crushing to black again this pair is the cause, and the contrast pass is the half to back off.
textures._comment_of11_shading: OF11. `normal_depth` 0.18 -> 0.45 and `ao_strength` 0.08 -> 0.2, both cut to those floors by EV4-hillside-seam-remainder-3 because a strong normal map was throwing the flank into self-shadow at a grazing sun. That was a real effect AT 8.3m PER TILE, where every normal feature was metres wide and shaded whole regions of hillside; at 2.2m per tile the same relief is fine-grained enough to average out with distance instead, so the fix and the defect are no longer the same trade. `tint` #fafafa -> #fff2e0 for the other half of that round's finding: a near-neutral grey under this scene's sky picks up the sky's own blue and a critic read the result as 'quite cool/blue-slate.' A near-white tint that suppresses blue slightly, rather than desaturating the photo further, is the correct answer to that and leaves the photo's own value range intact.
textures._comment_tint_r9_4: R9.4. Held at ~1.15x grass value for the same reason as soil. TUNABLE.
textures._comment_ev4_hillside_seam_remainder: EV4-hillside-seam-remainder. Was normal_depth 0.6 / ao_strength 0.4 -- the highest relief and the highest AO strength of any texture in this list, on a photo (Rock030_Color.jpg) that is already dark. At a grazing sun angle on a rise's curved flank, a normal map this strong throws much of the surface into self-shadow, and ao_strength this high darkens every crevice on top of that; together a blind critic read the result as 'a cast shadow wrapping the hill... could be mistaken for an ambient-occlusion artifact rather than a material,' not stone. Both cut well below grass's own 0.12/0.25 (rock keeps a little more relief than grass, 0.3 vs 0.12, but no longer the most aggressive AO in the set at 0.15 vs grass's 0.25) -- `tint` was already near-white and had no further room to brighten the read. TUNABLE; these were flagged untested by round 4 and are the first attempt at them.
textures._comment_ev4_hillside_seam_remainder_3: EV4-hillside-seam-remainder-3. `tint` had no headroom left (#fafafa is ~2% off pure white), so the further brightness lever this round needed is on the PHOTO itself: tools/art_pipeline/brighten_rock_texture.py applies a screen-blend lift to Rock030_Color.jpg in place; hue holds exactly (a uniform per-channel transform does not rotate hue) and saturation falls as a side effect. `normal_depth`/`ao_strength` cut again on top (0.3/0.15 -> 0.18/0.08) for the grazing-sun self-shadow the photo fix alone doesn't touch. Round 1 (LIFT_AMOUNT 0.18) shipped a real blind-critic-confirmed improvement -- a fresh critic on the round-1 render described the rock in one viewpoint as having 'more internal texture, light streaky veining' where round 0's critic saw 'no visible rock texture... a rendering artifact.' Round 2 pushed LIFT_AMOUNT to 0.24 and a critic then read the same material as 'quite cool/blue-slate' -- more desaturation than this scene's ambient lighting can carry before a neutral-grey material starts picking up the sky's own blue tint rather than reading as stone. Reverted to round 1's 0.18; the shading cut stays, the extra desaturation does not. Round 3 leaves rock alone and re-diagnoses soil instead -- see soil's own comment for what changed and why.

textures.name: soil
textures._comment_tint_ev4_hillside_seam_remainde: EV4-hillside-seam-remainder-3. Was #fafafa; rounds 1-2 tried #f0f0c8 then #ecec9c, pushing hue UP away from rock (toward yellow-olive) on the theory that soil/rock's shared hue (46-52 degrees, this item's own opening diagnosis) was the thing to fix. Both shipped real, measured movement in the OFFLINE photo x tint x colour-map chain (hue 51-54, saturation 0.37-0.50) but a blind critic on both renders still reported no visible tan/soil zone -- direct pixel sampling of the ACTUAL rendered frame (not the offline chain) explains why and is the real finding of this round: under this scene's real lighting, warm ground colours converge toward hue 50-60 regardless of their offline-computed hue -- close-three-quarter.png's own ground pixels (sky masked out via frame_stats.sky_mask) put ~87% of all ground area in that narrow band, ~145k-209k pixels, which is FAR more than the soil plateau's own geographic footprint could be on its own -- meaning grass's actual rendered hue and every 'push hue up' soil attempt were landing in the SAME real bucket. A critic seeing a more saturated version of grass's own hue reasonably reports 'no soil, just very green grass,' not 'a third material.' The direction was backwards: remainder's own round 2 (terrain_playground.json's `_comment_ev4_hillside_seam_remainder`, reverted for 'burnt orange/rust') pushed hue DOWN toward true tan/dirt (20-40 degrees) on the OLD, oversaturated photo (mean sat 0.45) and oversaturated into rust. remainder-2 fixed that photo (mean sat 0.45 -> 0.17) but nobody re-tried the down direction since -- #f0d5a8 does, more moderately: full chain lands at hue 39.6, saturation 0.473, value 0.438, inside the tan/dirt family without the old attempt's oversaturated photo underneath it. TUNABLE; if this still reads as grass, the next lever is colour.soil (untouched this round) rather than this tint alone.
textures._comment_tint_r9_4: R9.4. Rebalanced against the new grass value, not repainted. Soil is now ~1.35x grass in value instead of ~1.9x: the old ratio is what made the slope blends read as blown-out tan stripes rather than as ground (R7.1-found-3, and the blind critic's 'hard axis-aligned staircase' on frame 03). Hue is untouched -- warm dirt is exactly what the critic asked for MORE of. TUNABLE. Superseded below by EV4-hillside-seam-remainder-2's photo-level fix.
textures._comment_tint_ev4_hillside_seam: EV4-hillside-seam round 2. Was neutral grey #a4a4a4 -- a pure brightness scale with no hue shift, so Ground003_Color.jpg's own greenish weedy-lawn photo content stayed greenish, and a blind critic reading the baked hillside said the transition 'fades from black rock texture straight to green grass texture with no third element between them.' This is NOT the same attempt EV4 already tried and reverted -- that one warmed soil specifically to fake a close-range DIRT PATH (a much higher bar, since a path is scrutinised standing on it) and failed because the photo's own grass tufts show through at that distance regardless of tint. Soil is no longer used for paths at all (EV4 round 5 gave paths their own Ground030 texture); its only remaining job is the hillside slope band, judged from further away, where the bar is just 'reads as a third material, not grass and not rock' rather than 'reads as convincing dirt underfoot.' Suppresses blue/green relative to red so the underlying photo multiplies toward tan instead of stone-grey. TUNABLE. Superseded below.
textures._comment_ev4_hillside_seam_remainder: EV4-hillside-seam-remainder tried and REVERTED a stronger push here. Round 1 (soil_slope_deg 30->24, widening the pure-soil plateau -- see the `colour` block's own comment) did not make a distinct soil band visible: a fresh blind critic on the re-rendered frames still reported grass going straight to rock with nothing between, and direct pixel sampling of the transition zone measured hue 60-110 (yellow-green), not tan. Round 2 tried fighting Ground003_Color.jpg's own baked-in green content harder -- the same rock relief/AO cut (normal_depth 0.4->0.25, ao_strength 0.3->0.2) plus a stronger tint (#c9a874->#db9854) -- and a fresh blind critic on THOSE frames reported a NEW, worse defect: the whole hillside now read as 'burnt orange/rust/sienna... closer to a dead-autumn field than a grassy meadow slope,' ranked the single biggest gap from both reference boards, while the soil band was STILL not visible ('a hard grass-to-rock boundary with no intermediate dirt/soil material' in every frame). Reverted to the original values here -- soil_slope_deg 24 (round 1's widening) is kept since it caused no regression on its own, but pushing this texture's own tint/relief further just saturates a wider area of already-warm ground into a wrong colour without ever producing a visible third material. Two rounds, no soil-band improvement in either -- see EV4-hillside-seam-remainder-2 in BACKLOG.md for why this needs a different lever than tint.
textures._comment_ev4_reverted: EV4 tried tinting/de-relief-ing THIS texture warmer for paths across three rounds (rounds 2-3) and hit a wall: Ground003_Color.jpg is a photo of a weedy lawn with real green grass tufts painted into its own albedo, which no tint or normal_depth can repaint. Reverted to the original R9.4 values once EV4-textures' pre-sourced Ground030 (a real dirt/pebble pathway photo) gave paths their own dedicated texture instead -- this texture is back to doing only what it always did, hillside slope transitions, and carries no path-specific risk any more.
textures._comment_ev4_hillside_seam_remainder_2: EV4-hillside-seam-remainder-2. Two more failed rounds (see above) kept fighting the photo through this tint. Direct measurement finally explained why: Ground003_Color.jpg's OWN raw saturation (mean 0.45) was ~4.5x every sibling ground texture (Ground030 path 0.099, Rock030 0.126) -- the photo was oversaturated across nearly its whole area, not a narrow green patch. tools/art_pipeline/desaturate_soil_texture.py fixed the PHOTO itself (feathered blend toward local luminance, same technique as Ground030's moss fix, scaled to this photo's broader defect) -- but a first render afterward STILL measured rendered pixel saturation 0.65-0.76 in the soil band, far above the fixed photo's own 0.17 mean. Root cause: `colour.soil` below (a separate, EARLIER multiply layer over the whole soil band, meant to be 'near white... modulates rather than paints' per this file's own top comment) was ALSO warm and saturated (#e0cea4, sat 0.27), compounding with this tint (#c9a874, sat 0.42) on top of the photo -- the exact multiplicative-saturation bug R9.4 already diagnosed and fixed for grass elsewhere in this file, just not caught here yet. Simulated the real multiply chain (photo x tint x colour.soil) against 3000 sampled photo pixels before touching anything: tint=#fafafa (matching rock's own near-white-only-brightness convention, since the photo now carries the real colour and no longer needs fighting) + colour.soil desaturated below together land the simulated result at hue ~48, sat ~0.23 -- in the same family as rock's rendered read instead of nearly 3x hotter. TUNABLE, but re-tune the PAIR together (this tint and colour.soil) rather than either alone; they compound.

textures.name: path
textures._comment_ev4: EV4, round 5. ambientCG Ground030, sourced and ledgered independently by another lane while this ship's path-conversion work was in flight (see EV4-textures in DONE.md) -- a genuine dirt/pebble pathway photo, already breaking into grass at its own edges, unlike Ground003 above. Unlike grass/soil/rock, this did not need a hue-correcting tint: the photo's own colour is already the right family (muted warm grey-tan with sparse moss), so the tint here is a light near-white lift only, same philosophy as R9.4's 'let the texture carry the colour' rule for the other textures.
textures._comment_owner_round_2: Owner playtest report, second round, overrides EV4-textures' own stopping point below: 'paths need to be brown and look better.' EV4-textures round 3 already measured and named the residual defect (path reads paler than the references even with the moss/edge-stepping fixes) and left it alone deliberately, reasoning that desaturating further to fight moss had ALREADY once caused a worse defect ('closer to bone/sand/chalk'). That reasoning is sound for DESATURATING further, but it was never tested in the other direction. Close-range renders (shots/paths/grandpas-house-route.png) show the real photo detail (pebbles, worn-earth mottling) reading fine up close; the paleness is specifically a DISTANCE problem -- mid/long-range frames (shots/04-three-quarter.png) show the path reading as a flat pale yellow-green band once the photo's fine detail washes out under minification, at which point `tint` (a near-white #e4dac2, H39/S15%/V89%) is nearly all that is left driving the pixel's colour, and near-white does not read as dirt from far away no matter how good the close-up texture is. Raised tint saturation/warmth substantially (S15%->35%, V89%->65%, still hue ~30deg, the same warm family) so the path reads as brown at range even when the photo's own micro-detail has minified away, while leaving the photo itself (and its already-fixed moss regions) completely untouched -- this is the SAME 'let the texture carry it' lever EV4 already used, just pushed further now that the owner has explicitly said the previous stopping point was not enough.
textures._comment_ev4_textures: EV4-textures, three rounds, converged. Round 5's own moss patches (real detail in the source photo, hue ~97 deg, sat ~0.36 against the photo's own ~0.11 mean) measured to a blind critic as 'too saturated and too crisply circular... a texture-blend artifact rather than moss.' Round 1 tried a tint-only fix (a blue-lifted near-neutral, brute-force-searched to minimise moss saturation through the albedo_color multiply alone) -- moved the needle but a second blind critic named a NEW defect it caused: the whole path read 'too pale... closer to bone/sand/chalk' than trodden earth, because desaturating the WHOLE texture through one multiplier to chase the moss also flattened the dirt's own warmth. Rounds 2-3 fixed the actual pixels instead of fighting them through a multiply: `assets/environment/terrain/Ground030_Color.jpg` is CC0 (ASSET_LEDGER.md), so its moss regions (feathered-mask, hue 65-175 deg, sat>0.15 by round 3) are blended toward their own luminance in place -- taking the same measured moss patch's saturation 0.36 -> 0.13 (round 2) -> 0.09 (round 3, at/below the photo's own ~0.11 baseline), an effect no global tint could reach without also flattening the good 98% of the texture. `tint` reverted to the original warm #e4dac2 and `normal_depth` restored to 0.22 (round 5 shipped 0.25) once the pixels themselves carried the fix. A third blind critic confirmed real, described improvement ('no longer hard flat circles... softer-edged and less garishly saturated') and explicitly called the slope-edge-stepping half of this item resolved ('largely resolved... no rectangular notches or obvious staircasing'). What's left after three rounds is a softer, different complaint -- the moss blobs' own roughly-circular, similarly-sized SHAPE (real content in the source photo) still reads as 'a repeated stamped-decal layer' at close range, which no colour/saturation lever can fix; that's a content limit, not a tunable value, and is the honest place this item stops. Round 3 also turned up two defects outside this item's scope, both reproduced across all three critique rounds and worth carrying forward rather than losing: the path reads notably paler than the Palworld/key-art references even where the moss issue is fully resolved (edge-detail.png), and an unmotivated hard-edged shadow/overexposure band crosses the path in sunlit frames with no caster in shot -- see the new BACKLOG.md entry.
textures._comment_which: Chosen over Ground037 (also pre-sourced, damp mossy forest floor) because Ground037 is bible sec8's item 5 Deep Grass/Forest Floor, a different layer for under groves -- not the path. Ground037 is still unused; whoever wires up EV2/EV3's forest-floor layer should reach for it directly rather than re-sourcing.

river._comment: SE21, spec 3 Band 3 ('a substantial river divides the deeper Meadows'). Not a `crossing` and not a `spoke`: those are both single straight bars cut across one road, and this is a 340m channel with a bend in it that severs EVERY bearing it crosses. It is authored as a POLYLINE with a per-point cross-section -- playground_heightfield._river_carve walks the course the same way _stream_carve does and shapes it with the same smoothstep profile _carve_depth uses across and along, so there is still one falloff grammar on this map. Both ends run PAST world_perimeter's 235m ring (r=248 north, r=257 south), which is the property SC14's own `_comment_crossings_reach` said a real division needs and its gully could not have: there is no walking around either end, only the ring, and the only ground link between the near Meadows and the far bank is the Old Mill Crossing.
river._comment_depths: Depths are AUTHORED PER POINT against probed ground (tools/_probe_river.gd), not one number, because a single flat water plane has to sit in the finished bed from end to end. Target bed is about -15 through the wet reaches (ground runs -7.6 at the low middle, so the cut is the 10m floor there) and the cut is capped at 18m where the course climbs rises.peaks[0]'s south flank in the north (ground +19.5 at [199,-60]) -- so the bed rises above the water there and the last ~60m is a DRY gorge feeding the water, which is what the ground actually allows and is recorded here rather than pretended away. Every depth is at least 10m against a rim of 3.4-7m: 55-77 degrees of wall against the player's own 45-degree floor_max_angle (player.tscn), the same arithmetic every spoke gorge and the south gully are sized by. ALL TUNABLE.
river._comment_narrows: The five points from [166,32] to [158.6,52.2] are the Old Mill Crossing's narrows (SE22): the channel pinches from 22m wide to 7.2m at [162.4,42.1] and opens again over ~12m either side. That is not decoration -- it is what lets the crossing reuse the `south_bridge` prefab unchanged (an 18.4m span over a 14m clear gap: half_width 3.6 + rim 3.4, exactly the numbers here) instead of authoring a 34m river bridge no kit in this project owns. A river narrowing at the one place people built a mill and a bridge is also why such a place exists.
river._comment_water_level: ONE flat surface for the whole river (water.gd::_build_river), the pond's own mechanism rather than the stream's ribbon: the ribbon is monotone-clamped to descend, and a 340m course over ground that swings 27m cannot be both level and descending. -9.0 sits 1.5-6m below the natural grade of the low middle and south, so the water fills most of the channel and the visible bank is a couple of metres of earth -- a broad water that reads from the ridge -- and it thins to nothing as the bed climbs north. TUNABLE, but not independently of the depths above: raise it and the mid-course banks flood.
river._comment_failsafe: The channel is 10-18m deep with walls past the slope limit and there is no swimming system, so a player who walks in is stuck exactly the way SA4's probe found a body stuck in the storm ravine. river.gd hangs severed_spokes._add_carve_failsafe over each course segment with a VILLAGE-SIDE recovery point -- the same call and the same reasoning south_bridge.gd uses for its gully: recovering to the far bank would turn falling in into a free crossing.
river._comment_ow5c_rederive: OW5C, docs/MEADOWS_MACRO_LAYOUT.md section 9: re-derived per D46's supersession. Crosses the corridor's full width (x -1150..+1150, ~2321m of course including ~100m overrun past both x=+-1024 edges) at z~4080-4222, narrowing to the Old Mill Crossing's channel dimensions (half_width 3.6, rim 3.4, depth 15) at (-150,4203). Same order-of-magnitude depth/width as the old 18-point course (10-18 depth, 11-13 half_width away from the crossing) -- what divides the map is the course spanning the whole width with no gap, not extra depth. water_level/end_fade/failsafe unchanged.
